_readme: EXAMPLE FILE. The standing table: questions that recur across Ashby forms, answered once here instead of once per application. `ashby_yesno.mjs` and `press_all_pairs.mjs` answer pairs from it, `verify_and_submit.mjs` checks the page against it before submitting, and `ashby_finish_form.mjs` falls back to it. Format: `questionRe` is a case-insensitive regular expression matched against the question as the page words it, `answer` is the value to commit, and `note` says WHERE THE ANSWER COMES FROM. A rule without a note is a guess wearing a configuration file, so every rule here carries one - and so should every rule you add. `kind: "yesno"` marks a pair that must be answered as a pair. Fields also seen in the wild: `option` (commit this exact option text instead of a yes/no), `value` (free text), and `why` for a longer rationale than `note` allows.

That is a sentence you have to check against your own history; copied blindly it is a false statement on a real application.

EXAMPLE RULE - replace it. Required consent and agreement boxes are a standing Yes, because a form that asks for one cannot be submitted without it. Marketing and SMS consent are the exception and are NOT covered by this rule: those are a No unless you actually want the messages.

EXAMPLE RULE - replace it. Office and commute questions are a standing Yes for a candidate who will relocate. If a location question offers PLACES rather than Yes/No, do not answer it from this table at all - a place must come from the profile's own preference order, which is what the drafter's relocation path is for.

EXAMPLE RULE - replace it. `answer: "option"` commits the text in `option` rather than a yes/no, which is what a control offering a LIST needs. This entry is also the reason the file is not all yes/no: the helpers that answer pairs must recognise these and skip them, because pressing a place into a yes/no widget is how a form gets filled with the wrong kind of answer. If every rule you write is yes/no, that skip stops being exercised.
